ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: Homozygous parental white-eyed long-winged and red-eyed vestigial-winged fruit flies are crossed, with the results as shown in the figure. In F2, each phenotype has female and male individuals. On what chromosome is the gene controlling eye color located?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, the parental generation P is a cross between a white-eyed long-winged female fly and a red-eyed vestigial-winged male fly. In F1, females show red eyes and long wings, and males show white eyes and long wings; subsequently the F1 females and males mate. In F2, four phenotypes appear: white eyes and long wings, white eyes and vestigial wings, red eyes and long wings, red eyes and vestigial wings, with a ratio of 3:1:3:1; the question stem also states that each phenotype in F2 has female and male individuals. Then reason: The parents are homozygous. If the gene controlling eye color were located on an autosome, then after homozygous white-eyed and homozygous red-eyed individuals were crossed, the eye colors of F1 female and male individuals should be the same, and there should not be the sex difference of all females being red-eyed and all males being white-eyed. The eye-color expression of F1 in the figure is clearly related to sex: F1 females resemble the father in showing red eyes, and F1 males resemble the mother in showing white eyes. This conforms to X-linked inheritance: the white-eyed female parent can be represented as X^wX^w, and the red-eyed male parent can be represented as X^R Y; F1 females obtain X^R from the father and show red eyes, and F1 males obtain X^w from the mother and show white eyes. Therefore, the gene controlling eye color is located on the X chromosome.
